title: Arthritis and relationships: honest conversations that help (UK)
meta_description: How arthritis can affect relationships with partners, family and friends, and practical ways to talk honestly about pain, fatigue, roles and intimacy.
excerpt: How arthritis can affect relationships with partners, family and friends, and practical ways to talk honestly about pain, fatigue, roles and intimacy.
direct_answer: Arthritis can change roles, plans and intimacy in relationships. Talking honestly about how pain and fatigue vary, asking for specific help, and planning around better times can help. Couples counselling, such as Relate, and an occupational therapist or GP can offer further support.
author: Louis Maxwell
reviewer_credentials: First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member
keywords: arthritis relationships, partner, intimacy, sex and arthritis, talking to family, fatigue, carers, UK
content:
Arthritis affects more than joints. Pain, tiredness and changes in what you can do can affect your relationships with a partner, family and friends. Many people find it hard to talk about, but honest conversations can make a big difference.

This guide offers practical ideas for talking about arthritis and looking after relationships. It is educational information, not personal medical or relationship advice.

How arthritis can affect relationships

  • Pain and fatigue can change from day to day, which can be hard for others to understand.
  • Roles may change, for example who does the housework or drives.
  • Plans may need to change at short notice.
  • Pain, stiffness, tiredness and some medicines can affect sex and intimacy.
  • Partners and family may feel worried, frustrated or unsure how to help.

Talking to your partner or family

  • Choose a calm time to talk, not in the middle of a flare or an argument.
  • Explain that symptoms vary, and that a bad day is not about motivation.
  • Ask for specific help, such as "can you carry the shopping in", rather than general support.
  • Say what you want to keep doing yourself.
  • Listen to how they feel too.

Intimacy and sex

  • Plan intimacy for times when pain and stiffness are usually lower, or after pain relief has had time to work.
  • A warm bath or shower beforehand may ease stiffness.
  • Try different positions that put less strain on painful joints.
  • Remember that closeness and affection matter too.
  • If medicines or low mood affect desire, talk to your GP or rheumatology team.

Friends and social life

Explaining your condition simply, suggesting accessible plans, and keeping in touch by phone or video on difficult days can help friendships continue. Patient groups and online communities can also connect you with people who understand.

Getting support

Relate offers relationship counselling, including for couples dealing with illness. Your GP can refer you to talking therapies if low mood or anxiety is affecting you. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) has information on relationships and sex, and a helpline on 0800 5200 520. Partners who provide care can ask for a carer's assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you or someone else is in immediate danger.
  • Get urgent help if you are having thoughts of suicide: call NHS 111, your GP, or Samaritans on 116 123.
  • Contact the National Domestic Abuse Helpline on 0808 2000 247 if you feel unsafe in your relationship.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it normal for arthritis to affect our sex life?

Yes, it is common. Talking openly and asking your team for advice can help.

How do I explain fatigue?

Some people use the idea of a limited daily energy supply to explain why they need to pace activities.

What if my partner has become my carer?

It can change the relationship. Try to keep time for being a couple, and look into carer support and respite.
